question: How are task queues used for routing work to workers in this engine?
answer_hinglish:
Task queue ek simple naam hai (default "default") jo batata hai ki kaunsa worker kaunsa kaam uthayega. Is engine mein routing teen layer pe hoti hai: workflow ka task_queue, har activity ka optional task_queue, aur worker ke registered types.

Jab client `POST /workflows` karta hai, `StartIn.task_queue` (default "default") `workflows.task_queue` column mein store hota hai. Worker `python -m flowengine --task-queue X` se start hota hai aur `claim_workflow_task` sirf `task_queue = ANY(:q)` wale workflows claim karta hai. Saath mein `workflow_type = ANY(:t)` filter bhi hai -- yaani worker sirf woh workflow uthata hai jiska code uske process mein registered hai. Yeh important hai: agar worker ke paas code hi nahi hai toh replay kaise karega?

Activities ke liye `ctx.execute_activity(..., task_queue="gpu")` de sakte ho. `complete_workflow_task` activity task insert karte waqt `a["task_queue"] or current["task_queue"]` use karta hai -- matlab default mein activity workflow ki queue inherit karti hai. `claim_activity` bhi `task_queue = ANY(:q) AND activity_type = ANY(:t)` filter karta hai.

Interview mein point yeh hai: task queue ek logical address hai, physical server nahi. Isse aap specialised workers bana sakte ho -- jaise payment activities sirf PCI network wale workers pe, ya heavy image processing alag pool pe -- bina workflow code mein host names daale. Temporal mein bhi exactly yahi concept hai, bas wahan matching service queues ko partitions mein maintain karti hai; yahan yeh sirf Postgres column + filter hai.
why_needed: Bina routing ke har worker ko har workflow aur har activity ka code chahiye hoga, aur specialised resources (GPU, PCI zone, rate-limited API keys) ko isolate karna mushkil hoga.
real_world_analogy: Hospital ke counters: "cardiology", "ortho". Patient (task) counter ka naam dekh ke line mein lagta hai; jo doctor us counter pe baitha hai wahi use dekhega. Doctor kaun hai, patient ko farak nahi padta.
how_it_works: Workflow row mein task_queue; activity row mein task_queue (explicit ya inherited). Claim queries mein `= ANY(array)` filter + registered type filter. Worker ke multiple queues ho sakte hain (`--task-queue` append action).
in_this_project: `api.py::StartIn` mein `task_queue: str = "default"`. `store.py::claim_workflow_task` aur `store.py::claim_activity` dono `task_queue = ANY(:q)` aur type filter lagate hain. `worker.py::main` mein `ap.add_argument("--task-queue", action="append")`. `complete_workflow_task` mein `a["task_queue"] or current["task_queue"]` se activity ki queue decide hoti hai. Partial index `ix_workflows_pending ON workflows (task_queue, needs_task) WHERE status = 'running'` aur `ix_activity_ready (task_queue, visible_at)` queue-wise scan sasta rakhte hain.

# real, store.py::claim_activity (trimmed)
"WHERE id = (SELECT id FROM activity_tasks WHERE status = 'scheduled' AND visible_at <= now() "
"AND task_queue = ANY(:q) AND activity_type = ANY(:t) ORDER BY visible_at LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)"

# workflow code can route one activity elsewhere (illustrative)
await ctx.execute_activity("resize_image", url, task_queue="gpu")

Worker sirf woh claim karta hai jo woh run kar sakta hai (type filter)
Queue-wise partial indexes se scan sasta
disadvantages: Agar kisi queue pe koi worker nahi chal raha toh tasks chupchaap pade rahenge -- koi alert nahi
Queue naam typo = silent stuck work
common_mistakes: Activity ki queue set karna lekin us queue ka worker deploy na karna
Sochna ki task queue ek physical broker hai -- yahan woh sirf ek column filter hai

question: How do workers register themselves and report liveness, and what is that information used for?
answer_hinglish:
Har worker start hote hi `workers` table mein apni entry upsert karta hai aur phir har 5 second `_heartbeat_loop` se dobara upsert karke `last_heartbeat = now()` update karta hai. Stop pe `deregister_worker` row delete karta hai.

Entry mein kya hota hai: `worker_id` (hostname-pid-random), `task_queues`, `workflow_types`, `activity_types` (arrays), `started_at`, `last_heartbeat`. `register_worker` ek `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (worker_id) DO UPDATE` hai, isliye pehli call bhi aur baad ki heartbeat calls bhi same function hain.

Ab important baat: yeh information is project mein sirf VISIBILITY ke liye hai. `GET /workers` har worker ka `seconds_since_heartbeat` dikhata hai aur dashboard pe "Heartbeat age" column hai. Correctness kisi bhi tarah worker table pe depend nahi karti -- crash detection leases se hoti hai (`lease_until` on workflows aur activity_tasks), worker heartbeat se nahi. Yeh deliberate hai: agar correctness worker registry pe depend karti toh registry khud ek single point of truth ban jati jise consistent rakhna padta.

Ek honest gap: `kill -9` hua worker apni row delete nahi kar pata, aur koi cleanup job stale rows hataata nahi. Toh `/workers` pe dead worker ka heartbeat age badhta rehta hai -- operator ko khud filter karna padega (jaise age > 15s = dead). Production mein ek periodic cleanup ya TTL-based view add karna chahiye.
why_needed: Operators ko pata hona chahiye ki kitne workers zinda hain, kaun kaunsi queue serve kar raha hai -- warna "queue pe koi worker nahi" jaisi problem debug karna mushkil hai.
real_world_analogy: Office ka attendance register: har ghante sign karte ho. Register se HR dekh leta hai kaun aaya hai, lekin kaam kaun karega yeh register decide nahi karta -- woh task assignment (lease) se hota hai.
how_it_works: `Worker.run` -> `store.register_worker`; background `_heartbeat_loop` har 5s upsert; `finally` mein `deregister_worker`. API `extract(epoch FROM now() - last_heartbeat)` se age calculate karti hai.
in_this_project: `store.py::register_worker` upsert, `store.py::deregister_worker` delete, `worker.py::_heartbeat_loop` (`await asyncio.sleep(5)`), `api.py::workers` endpoint, `dashboard.html` workers table. Schema `workers (worker_id PK, task_queues text[], workflow_types text[], activity_types text[], started_at, last_heartbeat)` migration `0001_initial.py` mein. Observation: crashed worker ki row kabhi clean nahi hoti.
code_example:
# real, store.py::register_worker
"INSERT INTO workers (worker_id, task_queues, workflow_types, activity_types) VALUES (:i, :q, :w, :a) "
"ON CONFLICT (worker_id) DO UPDATE SET last_heartbeat = now(), task_queues = EXCLUDED.task_queues, "
"workflow_types = EXCLUDED.workflow_types, activity_types = EXCLUDED.activity_types"
advantages: Simple upsert, ek hi function registration aur heartbeat dono
Correctness registry pe depend nahi karti
Ops ko queue coverage dikhta hai
disadvantages: Dead workers ki rows stale reh jati hain
Heartbeat interval (5s) hard-coded hai
Koi alert built-in nahi
common_mistakes: Worker heartbeat ko task recovery ke liye use karna -- leases already per-task hain
Heartbeat ko DB transaction ke andar lamba hold karna
follow_up_questions: Worker heartbeat aur activity heartbeat mein kya fark hai?
Stale worker rows kaise clean karoge?
Kya queue ke liye 'no live worker' alert bana sakte ho?

question: If you had to design a durable workflow engine from scratch on a whiteboard, what components would you draw and why?
answer_hinglish:
Main whiteboard pe paanch cheezein draw karunga aur har ek ka "kyun" bataunga -- yeh basically flowengine ka design hai.

1. Append-only history store: har workflow ke facts (WorkflowStarted, ActivityScheduled/Completed, TimerFired, SignalReceived...) gap-free ordered event ids ke saath. Yeh single source of truth hai; state kabhi store nahi hota.

2. Deterministic replay runtime: workflow code ko shuru se chalao, history se results feed karo, naye commands nikalo. Isse koi bhi worker kisi bhi workflow ko continue kar sakta hai.

3. Do tarah ke task queues: workflow tasks ("is workflow ko replay karo, naye events aaye hain") aur activity tasks ("yeh side effect chalao"). Workflow task cheap aur pure CPU hai; activity mein real I/O aur retries.

4. Timer service: durable timers jo restarts survive karein -- due timer pe TimerFired event append.

5. Stateless workers: claim via leases (crash = lease expire = koi aur uthaye), fencing via attempt number, at-least-once activities ke saath idempotency key.

Plus client API: start (idempotent on workflow_id), signal, cancel, describe, history.

Hardest decision jo main explain karunga: commit protocol. Replay transaction ke bahar chalta hai, aur commit pe `last_event_id` compare hota hai -- agar beech mein signal aaya toh result discard. Isse lambe locks nahi, aur correctness determinism se aati hai.

Is project mein yeh sab ek Postgres mein hai (history, queues, timers). Scale pe main history ko workflow_id se shard karunga, matching ko alag service banaunga, aur polling ki jagah push/long-poll -- jaisa Temporal karta hai.
why_needed: Senior interviews mein "design X" ka matlab hai components + guarantees + failure handling + scaling ka narrative. Yeh project us narrative ka working proof hai.
real_world_analogy: Court ka case file: har hearing ka record (history) add hota hai, kabhi mitaya nahi jata. Naya judge aaye toh file shuru se padh ke wahi samajh banata hai (replay). Clerks (workers) badalte rehte hain, case file nahi.
how_it_works: Client -> API -> Postgres (workflows, history_events, activity_tasks, timers). Workers: workflow poller (claim -> replay -> optimistic commit), activity poller (claim -> execute -> complete/fail), timer+reaper loop, heartbeat loop.
in_this_project: `ARCHITECTURE.md` ka mermaid diagram exactly yeh components dikhata hai. `runtime.py::replay` runtime hai, `store.py` history/queues/timers, `worker.py::Worker` stateless worker, `api.py` client surface. `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` ka scaling table 10x/100x path deta hai.
code_example:
# illustrative: the whole engine in one loop per worker
while True:
    wf = claim_workflow_task()                 # SKIP LOCKED + lease, history 1..N
    outcome = replay(code, wf.history)         # pure CPU, no tx
    commit_if_last_event_id_still(N, outcome)  # optimistic
    act = claim_activity(); run(act, key=f"{wf_id}:{seq}"); record_result()
    fire_due_timers(); reap_expired_leases()
advantages: Har component ka single responsibility
Crash recovery design mein built-in
Audit trail free mein
disadvantages: Determinism ka bojh developer pe
Replay CPU cost history ke saath badhta hai
Ek DB = scale bottleneck
common_mistakes: Workflow state ko blob mein save karne ka design -- partial writes aur code changes pe toot jata hai
Workflow task aur activity task ko ek hi queue mein mila dena
follow_up_questions: History store ko kaise shard karoge?
Commit protocol optimistic kyun?
Exactly-once kahan possible hai aur kahan nahi?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Event history + replay vs state snapshot: replay robust hai aur audit deta hai, par CPU aur determinism cost hai. Single Postgres vs distributed store: simplicity vs throughput.
advanced.failure_scenarios: DB down = sab ruk jata hai (lekin kuch lost nahi). Worker crash = lease expiry tak delay. Bad deploy = non-determinism, workflows blocked.
advanced.alternatives: State-machine engines (AWS Step Functions JSON DSL), DAG schedulers (Airflow), BPMN engines (Camunda), ya Kafka pe choreographed sagas.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x: zyada worker processes, per-type queues, sticky cache. 100x: workflow_id se history shards, alag matching service, push delivery -- SYSTEM_DESIGN.md scaling table.
advanced.production_improvements: Versioning (patched), continue-as-new, payload encryption, namespaces/auth, metrics on backlog aur timer lag.

question: What does _settle do, and why is it a loop of asyncio.sleep(0) calls with a state comparison?
answer_hinglish:
`_settle` ka kaam hai workflow coroutine ko itna chalne dena jitna woh chal sakti hai -- jab tak woh sirf unresolved ctx futures pe atak na jaye. Replay mein har event feed karne ke baad hume yeh jaanna hai ki code ab "stable" hai, tabhi agla event dalein ya naye commands collect karein.

Problem: asyncio mein koi "coroutine ab blocked hai" wala direct API nahi hai. Ek future resolve hone ke baad bhi coroutine turant nahi chalti -- event loop ko ek ya zyada iterations chahiye (future callback schedule hota hai, phir task step hota hai, aur `asyncio.gather`/`asyncio.wait` jaise wrappers apne extra layers add karte hain).

Isliye `_settle` yeh karta hai: `asyncio.sleep(0)` teen baar (loop ko kuch iterations do), phir ek state tuple banao: `(task.done(), len(ctx.commands), sum(f.done() for f in ctx._futures.values()))`. Agar state pichhli baar jaisa hi hai, ya task khatam ho gaya, toh return. Warna phir se loop. Matlab "jab tak progress ho rahi hai, chalne do; jab do consecutive checks mein kuch na badle, maan lo settle ho gaya".

Yeh heuristic sirf tab sahi hai jab workflow code sirf ctx futures await kare. Agar koi `await asyncio.sleep(1)` ya HTTP call daal de, toh `_settle` uske complete hone se pehle hi return kar dega -- replay ka output timing pe depend karega, yaani non-deterministic. Yahi reason hai ki determinism rules mein "no I/O, no real sleep" hai. Temporal SDKs isko ek custom deterministic event loop se solve karte hain jo exactly jaanta hai ki koi runnable coroutine bachi hai ya nahi.
why_needed: Replay ko pata hona chahiye ki code kab ruk gaya, taaki agla history event sahi waqt pe feed ho aur naye commands ka set complete ho.
real_world_analogy: Dominoes ke chain ko dhakka diya; tum tab tak dekhte ho jab tak do baar dekhne pe koi naya domino na gire. Phir agla dhakka.
how_it_works: Loop: 3x `sleep(0)` -> snapshot (done, #commands, #resolved futures) -> compare with last -> equal ya done to return. Har history event ke baad aur shuru mein call hota hai.
in_this_project: `runtime.py::_settle` lines 189-198. `runtime.py::replay` shuru mein `await _settle(task, ctx)` karta hai aur har non-command event ke baad bhi. `tests/test_runtime.py::test_parallel_activities_with_gather` aur `test_race_signal_first_wins` (jismein `asyncio.wait` hai) prove karte hain ki multi-layer awaits bhi settle ho jate hain.
advantages: Standard asyncio pe chal jata hai, custom loop nahi likhna pada
Chhota aur testable
disadvantages: Heuristic hai: non-ctx awaits pe silently galat result
Signal futures (`_signal_waiters`) state tuple mein count nahi hote -- sirf commands aur `_futures`
Har event pe kuch extra loop iterations = CPU cost
common_mistakes: Workflow mein `asyncio.sleep` ya network call daalna aur sochna replay sahi chalega
Sirf ek `sleep(0)` ko kaafi maanna -- gather/wait layers ko zyada iterations chahiye
follow_up_questions: Temporal Python SDK custom event loop kyun use karta hai?
Agar workflow code thread pool use kare toh kya hoga?
State tuple mein signal waiters kyun nahi?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Std asyncio + heuristic = kam code, lekin guarantee nahi. Custom deterministic loop = strict, sandbox jaisa control, zyada complexity.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Workflow code mein real `asyncio.sleep` -> settle early return -> commands missing -> non-determinism ya stuck workflow. Bahut deep await chains (>3 layers per step) bhi extra loops lete hain lekin state compare unhe pakad leta hai.
advanced.alternatives: Temporal Python SDK ka custom `asyncio.AbstractEventLoop` jo sirf workflow ke tasks chalata hai aur timers ko virtual time mein; ya generator-based workflows (Durable Functions) jahan har `yield` explicit command hai.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Settle cost per event constant-ish hai lekin history lambi ho toh N events x settle = replay time badhta hai (TESTING.md: 2,001 events ~102-132 ms).
advanced.production_improvements: Deterministic event loop jo non-ctx await pe error throw kare; workflow sandbox jo `time`, `random`, network imports block kare.

question: Walk me through the replay() function line by line.
answer_hinglish:
`replay(fn, workflow_id, run_id, history)` ek pure function jaisa hai: input history, output `ReplayResult(status, new_commands, result, error)`. DB nahi chhoota.

Step 1: `history[0]` WorkflowStarted hai. Uske `created_at` se `WorkflowContext` banta hai (taaki `ctx.now()` start time de) aur `run_id` se seeded RNG.

Step 2: `asyncio.ensure_future(fn(ctx, input))` -- workflow coroutine task ban ke start hoti hai, `_settle` se chalne di jati hai jab tak woh pehle command pe block na ho.

Step 3: Baaki events recorded order mein. Har event pe pehle `ctx._now = ev["created_at"]`. Phir:
- `ActivityScheduled`/`TimerStarted`: yeh "command record" hai. Check: code ne isi seq pe same kind/activity_type produce kiya? Nahi toh `NonDeterminismError`. Haan toh seq ko `recorded` set mein daalo; settle nahi karna (kuch resolve nahi hua).
- `ActivityCompleted` -> `_resolve(seq, result)`; `ActivityFailed` -> `_resolve` with `ActivityError`; `TimerFired` -> resolve None.
- `SignalReceived` -> `_signal(name, payload)`; `CancelRequested` -> `_cancel()`.
- Workflow closed events -> break.
Har resolve ke baad `_settle`, taaki code aage chale aur naye commands produce kare.

Step 4: `new = commands jo recorded mein nahi` -- yahi naye commands hain jo store mein persist honge.

Step 5: task done hai? exception nahi = completed; WorkflowCancelled = cancelled; NonDeterminismError = raise; koi aur exception = failed. Task done nahi = blocked.

Step 6: `finally` mein agar task chal rahi hai toh cancel kar do -- coroutine discard, agli baar phir shuru se replay. Yahi "engine kabhi state store nahi karta" ka literal implementation hai.
why_needed: Yeh function poore engine ka dil hai -- determinism, races, cancellation, naye commands sab yahin decide hote hain. Interviewer isko line-by-line poochh sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Cricket match ki recording dobara dekhna: har ball (event) usi order mein chalao; scoreboard (state) khud ban jata hai. Agar recording mein ball aur tumhare script mein ball alag hai toh "yeh match hi alag hai" (non-determinism).
how_it_works: Init ctx -> start coroutine -> settle -> for each event: match command ya resolve+settle -> collect unrecorded commands -> classify status -> cancel leftover coroutine.
in_this_project: `runtime.py::replay` lines 201-252. `ReplayResult` dataclass status `blocked|completed|failed|cancelled`. Tests: `test_fresh_workflow_emits_first_command_only` (sirf WorkflowStarted -> ek new command), `test_replay_continues_from_history_and_completes`, `test_activity_failure_is_raised_in_workflow_code`, `test_non_determinism_detected_when_code_changes` -- sab `tests/test_runtime.py` mein bina DB ke.
code_example:
# real, runtime.py::replay (trimmed)
for ev in history[1:]:
    ctx._now = ev["created_at"]
    et, a = ev["event_type"], ev["attrs"]
    if et in ("ActivityScheduled", "TimerStarted"):
        ...  # determinism check against ctx.commands[a["seq"]]
        recorded.add(a["seq"]); continue
    if et == "ActivityCompleted":
        ctx._resolve(a["seq"], a.get("result"))
    ...
    await _settle(task, ctx)
new = [c for s, c in sorted(ctx.commands.items()) if s not in recorded]
advantages: Pure function: hand-built histories se unit test (10 tests, koi DB nahi)
Races recorded order se deterministic
Coroutine discard = koi stale in-memory state nahi
disadvantages: Har workflow task pe full replay (no sticky cache) -- cost history ke saath badhta hai
NonDeterminismError workflow code ke andar catch ho sakta hai agar code broad `except Exception` kare (sirf task exception pe re-raise hota hai)
common_mistakes: Sochna ki replay activities ko dobara execute karta hai -- nahi, sirf recorded results feed karta hai
ActivityScheduled pe settle karna -- zaroorat nahi, kuch resolve nahi hua
follow_up_questions: Closed events pe break kyun?
`recorded` set ka role kya hai?
Agar history mein completion hai lekin code ne command nahi diya toh?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Full replay har task pe: simple + always correct vs sticky cache: fast lekin cache invalidation, memory, eviction complexity.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Code exception = workflow failed (business failure). NonDeterminismError = workflow blocked (infra/deploy failure) -- dono ko alag treat karna sahi decision hai.
advanced.alternatives: Snapshotting (periodic state snapshot + replay from snapshot) -- lekin workflow coroutine ka state serialize karna Python mein practical nahi; isliye Temporal bhi sticky in-memory cache karta hai, snapshot nahi.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: TESTING.md: 21 events 0.5-2.1 ms, 201 events 3.4-12.6 ms, 2,001 events 102-132 ms -- super-linear. 100x events ke liye continue-as-new zaroori.
advanced.production_improvements: Sticky cache (last worker pe coroutine zinda rakho, sirf naye events feed karo), history size limit + continue-as-new, replay metrics (duration histogram).

question: How does _append guarantee gap-free, totally ordered event ids per workflow?
answer_hinglish:
`_append` ka contract hai: caller ne pehle hi workflow row lock (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) le rakha ho. Us lock ke andar woh `workflows.last_event_id` padhta hai, har naye event ke liye `last += 1` karke `history_events (workflow_id, event_id, ...)` mein insert karta hai, aur end mein `UPDATE workflows SET last_event_id = :l`.

Gap-free kyun? Kyunki id ek sequence/bigserial se nahi aa rahi. Postgres sequences transaction rollback pe numbers waste karte hain (gaps), aur concurrent transactions mein commit order aur number order alag ho sakta hai. Yahan id workflow row ke counter se aati hai jo row lock ke andar badhta hai -- toh do writers kabhi same workflow pe parallel append nahi kar sakte. Rollback hua toh counter update bhi rollback, koi gap nahi.

Totally ordered kyun? Ek workflow ke saare writers -- signal, cancel, activity complete/fail, timer fire, workflow task commit -- sab `_lock` se pehle row lock lete hain. Toh unka order lock acquisition order hai, aur event_id usi order ko reflect karta hai. `PRIMARY KEY (workflow_id, event_id)` extra safety net hai: agar koi bug se bina lock ke append kare toh duplicate id pe IntegrityError aayega, silent corruption nahi.

Yeh ordering kyun zaroori? Replay events ko event_id order mein feed karta hai. Signal vs timer race ka winner wahi hai jo pehle record hua. Agar ids ka order commit order se alag hota, toh do replays alag jawab de sakte the. Aur `last_event_id` hi optimistic commit ka version number bhi hai.
why_needed: Deterministic replay ke liye har workflow ki history ka ek fixed, unambiguous order chahiye -- aur optimistic concurrency ke liye ek monotonic version number.
real_world_analogy: Bank passbook mein entry number: clerk passbook haath mein leke (lock) agla number likhta hai. Do clerk ek saath ek passbook mein nahi likh sakte, isliye number kabhi skip ya repeat nahi hota.
how_it_works: Row lock -> read counter -> N inserts with counter+1.. -> write counter back -> commit. Per-workflow counter, global sequence nahi.
in_this_project: `store.py::_append` (lines 32-41) aur `store.py::_lock`. Callers: `start_workflow`, `signal`, `cancel`, `complete_workflow_task`, `complete_activity`, `fail_activity`, `fire_due_timers` -- sab pehle lock lete hain. Module docstring: "Every history append happens with the workflow row locked ... so events get gap-free, totally ordered ids per workflow." `DATABASE_DESIGN.md` table ki pehli row yahi explain karti hai.
code_example:
# real, store.py
async def _append(s, workflow_id: str, events: list[tuple[str, dict]]) -> int:
    """Caller must hold the workflow row lock. Returns the new last_event_id."""
    last = await s.scalar(text("SELECT last_event_id FROM workflows WHERE workflow_id = :w"), {"w": workflow_id})
    for et, attrs in events:
        last += 1
        await s.execute(text("INSERT INTO history_events (workflow_id, event_id, event_type, attrs) "
                             "VALUES (:w, :e, :t, CAST(:a AS jsonb))"), {...})
    await s.execute(text("UPDATE workflows SET last_event_id = :l WHERE workflow_id = :w"), {...})
    return last
advantages: Gaps nahi, rollback-safe
Ek hi counter ordering aur optimistic version dono deta hai
PK duplicate ko DB level pe rokta hai
disadvantages: Hot workflow (bahut signals) pe row lock contention
Har event alag INSERT -- batch insert nahi (97 statements/workflow ka ek hissa)
common_mistakes: Event id ke liye bigserial/sequence use karna -- gaps aur commit-order mismatch
Lock ke bina append call karna (docstring contract todna)

Sequence gaps se replay pe kya farak padta?

question: Explain the optimistic workflow-task commit protocol based on last_event_id.
answer_hinglish:
Workflow task teen phases mein chalta hai: claim, replay, commit -- aur sirf claim aur commit DB transactions hain, replay bahar.

Claim: `claim_workflow_task` ek transaction mein workflow pe lease leta hai (`locked_by`, `lease_until`) aur history `event_id <= last_event_id` (maan lo N) tak padhta hai. Transaction yahin khatam -- koi lock hold nahi.

Replay: pure CPU, bina transaction ke. Isi beech koi signal aa sakta hai, ya activity complete ho sakti hai -- woh events N+1, N+2 append karte hain aur `needs_task = true` set karte hain.

Commit: `complete_workflow_task` row lock leta hai aur check karta hai `current["last_event_id"] != wf["last_event_id"]` ya status running nahi. Agar history aage badh gayi, toh hamara result stale hai -- usne naya signal dekha hi nahi. Toh hum sirf apni lease release karte hain (`AND locked_by = :k` -- agar lease expire hoke kisi aur worker ke paas chali gayi hai toh usse nahi chhedte; yeh review fix hai), `needs_task` true hi rehta hai, aur `False` return. Agli baar koi worker poori nayi history ke saath replay karega. Agar match hai, toh ek hi transaction mein: naye command events append, activity_tasks aur timers insert, workflow close (agar finished), `needs_task = false`.

question: Walk through the claim_workflow_task SQL. What does each condition do?
answer_hinglish:
`claim_workflow_task` ek single `UPDATE ... WHERE workflow_id = (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) RETURNING *` hai, phir usi transaction mein history read.

Inner SELECT ke conditions:
- `status = 'running'` -- closed workflows pe kaam nahi.
- `needs_task` -- sirf woh workflows jinke paas naye events hain jo abhi replay nahi hue. Yahi boolean workflow-task queue hai.
- `task_queue = ANY(:q)` -- worker ki queues.
- `workflow_type = ANY(:t)` -- worker ke paas jiska code registered hai.
- `lease_until IS NULL OR lease_until < now()` -- koi aur worker abhi is pe kaam nahi kar raha, ya uski lease expire ho gayi (crash).
- `ORDER BY workflow_id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` -- ek row lo, jo row abhi kisi aur transaction ne lock ki hai use skip karo, wait mat karo.

Outer UPDATE: `locked_by = worker_id`, `lease_until = now() + lease_seconds` (default 10s, `FLOW_WORKFLOW_TASK_LEASE_SECONDS`). `RETURNING *` se `last_event_id` mil jata hai.

Phir history: `event_id <= :n` jahan n = returned last_event_id. Yeh important hai -- hum exactly woh snapshot padhte hain jiske against commit check hoga.

Note karo `needs_task` claim pe clear nahi hota -- woh commit pe clear hota hai. Agar worker crash ho jaye, lease expire hote hi workflow phir claimable hai. Ek observation: `ORDER BY workflow_id` FIFO nahi hai -- alphabetically chhote ids hamesha pehle; heavy load pe kuch workflows starve ho sakte hain. Production mein `ORDER BY` kisi "ready since" timestamp pe hona chahiye.
why_needed: Many workers ko duplicate work ke bina, bina blocking ke, aur crash-safe tareeke se workflow tasks baantne hain.
real_world_analogy: Ticket counter pe "jo khidki khali hai wahan jao, jahan koi khada hai use chhod do" (SKIP LOCKED), aur token pe 10 minute ka time likha hai (lease) -- time khatam toh koi aur le sakta hai.
how_it_works: Atomic claim+lease UPDATE, SKIP LOCKED for non-blocking concurrency, lease for crash recovery, history read bounded by returned version.

question: Walk through claim_activity. Why attempt + 1 at claim time, and how is the lease computed?
answer_hinglish:
`claim_activity` bhi same pattern hai: `UPDATE activity_tasks SET ... WHERE id = (SELECT id ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) RETURNING *`.

Inner SELECT: `status = 'scheduled' AND visible_at <= now()` -- sirf ready tasks; retry backoff ke dauran `visible_at` future mein hota hai toh task invisible rehta hai. Plus `task_queue` aur `activity_type` filters, `ORDER BY visible_at` (jo pehle ready hua woh pehle -- roughly FIFO).

Outer UPDATE:
- `status = 'started'`
- `attempt = attempt + 1` -- attempt claim pe badhta hai, completion pe nahi. Kyun? Kyunki attempt hi fencing token hai. Agar worker A ka lease expire hua aur B ne claim kiya, B ka attempt 2 hai; A jab late complete karne aaye toh `WHERE attempt = 1` match nahi karega. Aur crash wala attempt bhi count hota hai -- maximum_attempts sahi kaam karta hai.
- `locked_by = worker_id`
- `lease_until = now() + coalesce(heartbeat_timeout_seconds, start_to_close_seconds) + 1` -- agar activity heartbeat karti hai toh lease chhota (heartbeat timeout), warna poora start_to_close. +1 second network/scheduling slack ke liye.
- `last_heartbeat_at = now()`.

Heartbeat wala lease is project ke ek real bug ka fix hai: pehle heartbeat lease ko start_to_close (30s) se extend kar raha tha, toh dead worker 30s baad detect hota tha; ab heartbeat timeout (test mein 0.5s) se.

question: How does fail_activity decide between retry and permanent failure, and what does 'stale' mean?
answer_hinglish:
`fail_activity(sm, task, error, error_type, timed_out=False)` teen me se ek return karta hai: `'retry'`, `'failed'`, `'stale'`.

Pehle decision (DB ke bahar): `policy = RetryPolicy.from_json(task["retry"])` aur `final` true hai agar (a) `error_type` policy ke `non_retryable_errors` list mein hai, ya (b) `error_type == "NonRetryableError"`, ya (c) `maximum_attempts` set hai (0 = unlimited) aur `attempt >= maximum_attempts`.

Phir transaction: pehle workflow row lock (`_lock`) -- kyunki failed case mein history append hoga, aur saare writers same lock order follow karte hain. Lock ke turant baad `_closed()` guard: workflow ab running nahi (cancel/complete) toh task cancelled aur 'stale' -- closed workflow ki activity kabhi retry nahi hoti (review fix).

Retry path: `UPDATE activity_tasks SET status='scheduled', locked_by=NULL, lease_until=NULL, last_error=..., visible_at = now() + delay WHERE id=:i AND status='started' AND attempt=:a`. `delay = min(initial * coeff^(attempt-1), maximum_interval) * random.uniform(0.8, 1.2)` -- +-20% jitter review fix hai, taaki ek saath fail hui activities lockstep mein retry na karein. Koi history event nahi likha jata -- retries workflow ko dikhte hi nahi, sirf final outcome. Yeh Temporal jaisa hai: workflow history retries se nahi phoolti.

Final path: status `'failed'`, phir `ActivityFailed` event append (seq, activity_type, error, error_type, attempts, timed_out) aur `needs_task = true` -- workflow replay hoke `ActivityError` apne code mein catch karega.

`'stale'`: dono UPDATEs `AND attempt = :a AND status = 'started'` se fenced hain. Agar rowcount 0 hai, matlab hum ab owner nahi -- lease expire hui, reaper ne already retry kar diya, ya kisi aur attempt ne complete kar diya. Tab hum kuch nahi likhte. Reaper isi function ko `ActivityTimeout` ke saath call karta hai, aur stale ko count nahi karta.
why_needed: Retry logic ko central aur fenced hona chahiye -- warna crash ke baad do workers dono "fail" record karke double retries ya galat ActivityFailed bana sakte hain.
real_world_analogy: Courier delivery fail: agar "address galat" (non-retryable) toh return to sender; "ghar band tha" toh kal phir try, har baar thoda baad; teen baar ke baad bhi nahi toh return. Aur agar package already doosre delivery boy ko re-assign ho gaya, purane ki report ignore.

question: What happens inside complete_activity, and why does it lock the workflow row?
answer_hinglish:
Activity successfully chali, worker `store.complete_activity(sm, task, result)` call karta hai. Ek transaction mein teen kaam:

0. `_closed(s, wf, task)` -- lock ke baad pehla check: workflow ab `running` nahi (cancel/complete ho chuka) toh task `cancelled` mark aur `return False`, history mein kuch nahi.

1. `_lock(s, workflow_id)` -- workflow row `FOR UPDATE`. Kyun activity complete karne ke liye workflow lock? Kyunki hume `ActivityCompleted` history event append karna hai, aur history append ka rule hai "row lock ke andar hi" taaki event ids gap-free aur ordered rahein. Plus saare writers ka lock order same hai (pehle workflow), toh deadlock risk kam.

2. Fenced update: `UPDATE activity_tasks SET status='completed', lease_until=NULL WHERE id=:i AND status='started' AND attempt=:a`. Agar rowcount 0 -- matlab hamari lease expire ho gayi aur reaper ne task wapas scheduled kar diya ya naye attempt ne le liya -- toh `return False`. Worker `stats["stale"]` badhata hai. Is case mein activity ka side effect ho chuka hai, lekin idempotency key (`workflow_id:seq`) same hai, toh next attempt ka effect `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` se duplicate nahi hoga.

3. `ActivityCompleted {seq, result}` append, aur `UPDATE workflows SET needs_task = true WHERE ... AND status = 'running'` -- workflow task trigger.

Review story: pehle append `status = 'running'` check nahi karta tha -- agar workflow beech mein cancel/complete ho chuka tha (aur activity already 'started' thi), toh `ActivityCompleted` closed workflow ki history mein `WorkflowCompleted` ke BAAD append ho jaata. Fix: `_closed()` guard `complete_activity` aur `fail_activity` dono mein (fail_activity 'stale' lautata hai). Regression test `test_late_activity_completion_after_close_appends_nothing` -- late complete False, late fail 'stale', history length same.

question: What does the worker's timer loop do: how are timers fired and expired activity leases reaped?
answer_hinglish:
`Worker._timer_loop` har poll interval pe do kaam karta hai: `fire_due_timers` aur `reap_expired_activities`. Har worker yeh loop chalata hai -- koi alag scheduler process nahi.

`fire_due_timers(limit=100)`: pehle bina lock ke `SELECT workflow_id, seq FROM timers WHERE NOT fired AND fire_at <= now() ORDER BY fire_at LIMIT 100`. Phir har timer ke liye alag transaction: workflow row lock, `UPDATE timers SET fired = true WHERE ... AND NOT fired`. Agar rowcount 1 aur workflow running hai, toh `TimerFired {seq}` append aur `needs_task = true`. Multiple workers same timer dekh sakte hain, lekin `AND NOT fired` + row lock guarantee karta hai ki sirf ek hi fire karega. Observation: SKIP LOCKED nahi hai, toh workers ek doosre ke lock pe wait kar sakte hain -- correctness theek, efficiency kam.

`reap_expired_activities`: `SELECT * FROM activity_tasks WHERE status = 'started' AND lease_until < now() LIMIT 100`, aur har ek pe `fail_activity(..., "lease expired (worker crashed, hung, or missed heartbeats)", "ActivityTimeout", timed_out=True)`. Matlab expired lease = ek timed-out attempt; retry policy normal tarah apply hoti hai. Fencing (`attempt = :a`) ki wajah se agar asli worker usi waqt complete kar raha ho toh ek hi jeetega.

Errors loop ko nahi maarte -- `try/except Exception: log.exception("timer_loop_error")`. Timer precision = poll interval (default 0.1s) + timer creation mein worker clock vs DB clock ka skew (fire_at worker ke `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` se banta hai, compare DB `now()` se).

question: How does complete_workflow_task turn replay output into events, activity tasks and timers?
answer_hinglish:
Optimistic check pass hone ke baad `complete_workflow_task` ek hi transaction mein replay ke `ReplayResult` ko durable banata hai.

Error path pehle: agar `outcome is None` (replay hi NonDeterminismError se fail hua), toh workflow ko fail NAHI karte. Sirf `error` column set, `needs_task = false`, lease release. Workflow running rehta hai, blocked -- code fix/rollback ke baad resume ho sake. Temporal bhi yahi karta hai.

Normal path, har new command ke liye:
- `schedule_activity` -> `ActivityScheduled {seq, activity_type, args, retry}` event aur `activity_tasks` mein row (status scheduled, retry jsonb, start_to_close, heartbeat_timeout, task_queue = command ki ya workflow ki).
- `start_timer` -> `fire_at = now + seconds`, `TimerStarted {seq, seconds, fire_at}` event aur `timers` row.

Phir agar status completed/failed/cancelled hai toh closing event (`WorkflowCompleted {result}` / `WorkflowFailed {error}` / `WorkflowCancelled`) bhi list mein. Ek `_append` call sab events ko consecutive ids deta hai. Close pe `workflows` row mein status, result, error, `closed_at`, `needs_task=false`, lease clear, aur bache hue `scheduled` aur `started` activity tasks cancel (started wala review fix hai -- pehle sirf scheduled). Not closed: `needs_task=false, error=NULL`, lease clear.

Key insight: command event, task row aur timer row ek hi transaction mein hain -- "event likha lekin task nahi bana" possible nahi. `UNIQUE (workflow_id, seq)` on activity_tasks aur timers PK extra guard hai ki ek command do baar schedule na ho. Observation: `fire_at` worker ke Python clock se aata hai, jabki event ka `created_at` DB `now()` hai.

real_world_analogy: Manager ka meeting decision: minutes mein likhna (event) aur tasks Jira mein banana (activity_tasks) ek saath hona chahiye -- warna minutes mein hai lekin kisi ko kaam mila hi nahi.
how_it_works: Lock + version check -> map commands to (event, row) pairs -> optional close event -> single `_append` -> update workflow row (close ya clear needs_task).

question: How is wait_signal with a timeout implemented, and why does it call timer.result() at the end?
answer_hinglish:
`ctx.wait_signal(name, timeout)` ke teen raaste hain.

1. Buffer check: `q = self._signal_queues.setdefault(name, [])`; agar queue mein pehle se payload hai (signal code ke wait karne se pehle aa chuka tha), toh turant `q.pop(0)` return. Yahi signal buffering hai -- `test_signal_before_waiting_is_buffered`.

2. Nahi toh ek plain future banta hai aur `_signal_waiters[name]` mein add hota hai. Timeout None hai toh bas `await fut`.

3. Timeout diya hai toh `timer = self.sleep(timeout)` -- yeh ek normal durable timer command hai (TimerStarted event banega). Phir `asyncio.wait({fut, timer}, return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED)`. Jo pehle resolve hua woh jeeta. Replay mein "pehle" ka matlab hai history mein pehle record hua -- kyunki replay events ek-ek karke feed karta hai aur har ek ke baad settle karta hai. Isliye race deterministic hai (`test_race_signal_first_wins`, `test_race_timer_first_wins`).

Signal jeeta: `fut.result()` return. Timer jeeta: waiter ko list se hata do (warna baad wala signal is mare hue future ko de diya jata aur kho jata -- ab woh buffer mein jayega), phir `timer.result()`, phir `None` return.

`timer.result()` kyun? Timer future do tarah se done ho sakta hai: TimerFired se (result None) ya cancellation se (`_cancel` usme `WorkflowCancelled` set karta hai). `.result()` call karne se cancel wala exception re-raise hota hai -- warna cancel ko "timeout" samajh ke workflow galat branch (jaise refund) le leta.

Observation: signal jeetne pe timer cancel nahi hota; `timers` row baad mein fire hoke ek extra `TimerFired` append karti hai aur ek extra workflow task trigger hota hai (`_resolve` done future pe return kar deta hai, toh harmless).
why_needed: Business processes mein "approval aaye ya X time ho jaye" sabse common pattern hai; isko deterministic aur cancel-aware hona chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Cab booking: driver accept kare ya 2 minute ho jaye. Jo pehle hua woh final. Aur agar beech mein tum hi booking cancel kar do, toh woh "timeout" nahi, "cancelled" hai.
how_it_works: Buffer -> waiter future -> durable timer -> asyncio.wait FIRST_COMPLETED -> cleanup waiter -> timer.result() to propagate cancel.

Tests: `tests/test_runtime.py::test_race_signal_first_wins`, `test_race_timer_first_wins`, `test_signal_before_waiting_is_buffered`.

question: Why does _resolve raise NonDeterminismError when the future is missing, and why does it silently return when the future is already done?
answer_hinglish:
`_resolve(seq, result, exc)` history ke completion events (ActivityCompleted/Failed, TimerFired) ko workflow ke future tak pahunchata hai.

Future missing (`self._futures.get(seq)` None): matlab history kehti hai "command seq 3 complete hua", lekin current code ne replay mein seq 3 kabhi issue hi nahi kiya. Yeh tabhi hota hai jab code badal gaya -- koi step hata diya, ya branch alag chali. Normally `ActivityScheduled`/`TimerStarted` check pehle hi pakad leta hai, lekin `_resolve` ek second safety net hai: chupchaap ignore karna sabse khatarnak hota, kyunki workflow ek result kho deta aur aage galat state mein chalta. Isliye hard error: `NonDeterminismError("history has a completion for command N, which the code never issued")`.

Future already done: `if fut.done(): return`. Yeh kab hota hai? Do realistic cases:
1. Cancellation: `_cancel()` ne pending futures mein `WorkflowCancelled` set kar diya, phir history mein us activity ka late `ActivityCompleted` aaya (activity already chal rahi thi). Result ignore -- code already cancellation handle kar raha hai. (Review fix ke baad `store.cancel` running task ko bhi `cancelled` mark karta hai aur uska completion fenced hai, toh naye runs mein yeh late event history mein aana bahut kam hai -- par purani histories aur defense in depth ke liye guard zaroori hai.)
2. Losing timer: `wait_signal(timeout)` mein signal jeet gaya; timer row baad mein fire hoti hai aur `TimerFired` aata hai. Future pehle se done nahi hai actually -- timer future pending hi hai, toh woh resolve hoga lekin koi await nahi kar raha, harmless.

`set_result` ek done future pe `InvalidStateError` throw karta, toh yeh guard zaroori hai. Design lesson: replay ke engine-side handlers ko "events jo ab irrelevant hain" ke liye tolerant hona chahiye, lekin "events jo code se match hi nahi karte" ke liye strict.
why_needed: History aur code ke beech mismatch ko silently swallow karna data corruption hai; lekin legit late events pe crash karna bhi galat hai. Yeh function dono ko alag karta hai.
real_world_analogy: Courier aata hai parcel ke saath: agar tumne kabhi order hi nahi kiya (missing future) -- alarm. Agar order cancel kar chuke ho aur parcel ab aaya (done future) -- bas side mein rakh do.
how_it_works: Lookup future by seq -> missing: raise -> done: ignore -> else set_exception/set_result.

question: How do the @workflow and @activity decorators work, and how does a worker know what it can run?
answer_hinglish:
Dono decorators simple global registries hain. `runtime.py` mein `WORKFLOWS: dict[str, WorkflowFn] = {}` aur `workflow(name)` decorator function ko `WORKFLOWS[name] = fn` mein daal deta hai. Same `activities.py` mein `ACTIVITIES` aur `activity(name)`. Naam string hai -- yahi naam history mein (`workflow_type`, `activity_type`) aur DB rows mein jata hai, Python function ka naam nahi.

Registration import time pe hota hai. Isliye `flowengine/examples/__init__.py` `from . import activities, workflows` karta hai, aur `main.py` aur `worker.py::main` dono `from . import examples` import karte hain -- "importing this package registers them".

Worker ko kaise pata kya chala sakta hai? `Worker.__init__` mein `self.workflows = workflows if ... else WORKFLOWS` aur same activities. Phir:
- `register_worker` mein `sorted(self.workflows)` aur `sorted(self.activities)` workers table mein jate hain (visibility).
- `claim_workflow_task(..., sorted(self.workflows))` -> SQL `workflow_type = ANY(:t)`.
- `claim_activity(..., sorted(self.activities))` -> `activity_type = ANY(:t)`.
Toh worker kabhi aisa task claim hi nahi karta jiska code uske paas nahi.

API side: `POST /workflows` mein `if body.workflow_type not in WORKFLOWS: raise Unprocessable(...)` -- unknown type 422 with list of known types. Security angle: sirf registered names hi execute hote hain; input JSON data hai, code nahi.

Name ko stable rakhna zaroori hai -- function rename karo koi baat nahi, lekin registry name badla toh purane running workflows ka code kahin nahi milega.

question: What does ActivityContext contain, and how is the heartbeat function wired up in Worker._execute?
answer_hinglish:
`ActivityContext` ek dataclass hai jo har activity ke pehle argument ke roop mein milta hai: `workflow_id`, `activity_type`, `seq`, `attempt`, `idempotency_key`, `sm` (session maker -- activity khud DB use kar sake) aur private `_heartbeat` callable. Public method `async heartbeat(details=None) -> bool`.

`Worker._execute` isko aise banata hai:
```
ActivityContext(task["workflow_id"], task["activity_type"], task["seq"], task["attempt"],
f"{task['workflow_id']}:{task['seq']}", self.sm,
lambda d=None: store.heartbeat(self.sm, task["id"], task["attempt"], d))
```
Do important baatein:

1. `idempotency_key = workflow_id:seq` -- attempt number shamil NAHI hai. Isliye har retry aur redelivery pe key same rehti hai. Activity ise payment provider ko de ya `activity_effects` mein unique key bana de -> side effect ek hi baar.

2. Heartbeat lambda `task["id"]` aur `task["attempt"]` capture karta hai. `store.heartbeat` SQL `WHERE id = :i AND status = 'started' AND attempt = :a` -- yaani heartbeat bhi fenced hai. Return `rowcount == 1`. Agar False aaya, matlab hamari lease expire ho chuki aur task kisi aur attempt ka hai -- activity ko kaam rok dena chahiye. `examples/activities.py::long_task` exactly yahi karta hai: `if not await ctx.heartbeat({"done": i + 1}): return None`.

Heartbeat lease ko `coalesce(heartbeat_timeout_seconds, start_to_close_seconds) + 1` se extend karta hai aur `heartbeat_details` jsonb mein progress save karta hai. Gap: woh details agle attempt ko ActivityContext mein nahi milti, toh `long_task` retry pe chunk 0 se shuru hota hai.
why_needed: Activity ko teen cheezein chahiye: stable idempotency key, apni identity (attempt), aur engine ko "zinda hoon" bolne ka tareeka jo fencing bhi bataye.
real_world_analogy: Delivery boy ka app: order id (idempotency key) har attempt pe same; har 5 minute location ping (heartbeat); agar app bole "yeh order ab tumhara nahi", ruk jao.

question: How does Worker._execute map activity outcomes and exceptions to engine calls?
answer_hinglish:
`_execute(task)` activity ko chalata hai aur outcome ko teen raaston mein map karta hai.

Run: `result = await asyncio.wait_for(fn(ctx, *task["input"]), task["start_to_close_seconds"])`. Input jsonb list hai jo positional args ban jati hai.

1. `asyncio.TimeoutError` -> start_to_close exceed hua. `store.fail_activity(..., f"exceeded start_to_close {n}s", "ActivityTimeout", timed_out=True)`. `wait_for` activity coroutine ko cancel bhi kar deta hai. Retry policy normal apply -- timeout ek retryable failure hai (jab tak "ActivityTimeout" non_retryable list mein na ho).

2. Koi bhi `Exception` -> `etype = "NonRetryableError" if isinstance(exc, NonRetryableError) else type(exc).__name__`. Yaani error type class ka naam hai, jaise `ConnectionError`, `RuntimeError`. `fail_activity` isi naam ko policy ke `non_retryable_errors` list se match karta hai. NonRetryableError subclass ko bhi explicitly "NonRetryableError" bana diya jata hai taaki subclass bhi non-retryable rahe.

3. Success (`else`) -> `store.complete_activity`; True to `activities_ok++`, False (fenced) to `stale++`.

Stats aur structured logs (`activity_timeout`, `activity_failed` with workflow_id, seq, outcome) dono update hote hain.

Kya NAHI pakda jata: `asyncio.CancelledError` (BaseException). Jab `Worker.kill()` running tasks cancel karta hai, `_execute` kuch record nahi karta -- bilkul crash jaisa. Lease expire hogi aur reaper ise timeout attempt maanega. Yeh deliberate hai, kill ko real crash simulate karna hai. Graceful stop mein bhi grace ke baad pending tasks cancel hote hain -- "lease expiry will hand them to another worker".

real_world_analogy: Factory supervisor: kaam time pe khatam nahi hua -> "timeout" report; machine kharab (retryable) -> phir try; raw material hi galat (non-retryable) -> reject. Supervisor bhaag gaya -> koi report nahi, shift timer khatam hone pe pata chalega.

question: Look at _cancel and _future: which futures are failed on cancellation, and why are futures created afterwards left alone?
answer_hinglish:
`_cancel()` teen kaam karta hai: `cancel_requested = True`, aur us moment pe jitne futures pending hain -- `self._futures` ki saari values (activities, timers) plus saare `_signal_waiters` -- un sab mein `set_exception(WorkflowCancelled())` agar done nahi hain. List pehle snapshot hoti hai (`list(...)`) -- dict iterate karte hue modify nahi.

Ab `_future(seq)` dekho: yeh bas naya future banata aur `_futures` mein daalta hai, `cancel_requested` check NAHI karta. Comment explicitly kehta hai: "futures created AFTER cancellation work normally -- that is how compensation activities run. Only what was pending at the moment of cancellation is failed."

Kyun? Workflow code yeh likhta hai:
```
except WorkflowCancelled:
await ctx.execute_activity("notify", ..., "review cancelled")
raise
```
Compensation ek naya activity hai jo cancel ke BAAD schedule hota hai. Agar `_future` cancel_requested dekh ke turant fail kar deta, toh compensation kabhi chal hi nahi sakti thi -- har naya await bhi WorkflowCancelled throw karta. Yahi is project ka bug #1 tha (FAILURE_SCENARIOS.md: "After cancellation, NEW futures were failed too, so compensation activities could never run").

Semantics Temporal jaisa hai: cancellation ek ek-baar ka "interrupt" hai jo current awaits mein deliver hota hai; uske baad workflow apna cleanup normal tarah kar sakta hai, aur phir ya toh `raise` karke cancelled status leta hai ya return karke completed.

question: How does email_campaign run parallel activities with asyncio.gather, and how does replay handle them?
answer_hinglish:
`email_campaign` recipients ko `batch_size` ke batches mein todta hai. Har batch ke liye:
```
results = await asyncio.gather(*[ctx.execute_activity("send_email", r, inp["template"], retry=FAST) for r in batch],
return_exceptions=True)
```
`execute_activity` turant (synchronously) seq number lekar ek command record karta hai aur future return karta hai. List comprehension batch ke saare commands ek saath bana deta hai -- seq 1,2,3... deterministic order mein (recipients list ka order). Phir gather sab futures pe wait karta hai. Ek hi workflow task mein saare commands `new_commands` mein jate hain, `complete_workflow_task` sabke ActivityScheduled events aur activity_tasks ek transaction mein banata hai -- aur workers unhe parallel chalate hain (`activity_concurrency`).

`return_exceptions=True` kyun? Bounced address (`send_email` "bounce" -> NonRetryableError -> ActivityFailed -> ActivityError) poore campaign ko fail na kare. Result loop `isinstance(out, ActivityError)` check karke `failed` list mein daalta hai, warna `sent += 1`.

Batches ke beech `await ctx.sleep(inp["pause"])` -- durable timer, last batch ke baad nahi.

Replay mein: completions kisi bhi order mein aa sakti hain (activity 3 pehle, 1 baad mein) -- history mein jo order record hua usi order mein `_resolve` hoga. Gather tabhi resolve hota hai jab sab done, toh final result order-independent hai. `test_parallel_activities_with_gather` prove karta hai ki fresh replay teen commands `["a"], ["b"], ["c"]` deta hai. E2E `test_email_campaign_parallel_batches`: 7 recipients, batch 3 -> `{"sent": 6, "failed": ["bounce@x.io"], "batches": 3}` aur email effect exactly 6.

question: Walk me through the order_processing workflow code.
answer_hinglish:
`order_processing` ek saga hai: reserve -> charge -> ship -> confirm, aur failure pe compensations. Sab activities `FAST` retry policy (initial 0.05s, max 0.5s, 3 attempts) use karti hain.

Step 1: `res = await ctx.execute_activity("reserve_inventory", inp["items"])` -- reservation_id milta hai (activity idempotency key hi reservation id ban jati hai).

Step 2: charge `try` ke andar. `except ActivityError as e:` -> `release_inventory(res["reservation_id"])` aur `return {"status": "payment_failed", "reason": e.message}`. Note: yeh return karta hai, raise nahi -- business outcome "payment failed" ek successful workflow completion hai, failure nahi.

Step 3: ship `try` ke andar. Fail -> compensations reverse order mein: pehle `refund_payment(charge_id, amount)`, phir `release_inventory`. Return `{"status": "compensated", ...}`.

Step 4: `send_email(customer, "order_confirmed")`, return `{"status": "completed", "tracking": ..., "charge_id": ...}`.

Kya dekhna hai: koi state machine, koi DB flags, koi "step" column nahi. Workflow ka state local variables (`res`, `charge`) hain jo replay se rebuild hote hain. Aur compensation durable hai -- agar refund ke beech worker crash ho, koi aur worker replay karke wahin se continue karega. Hand-written sagas ki sabse badi kamzori (crash ke baad compensation bhool jana) yahan nahi hai.

Tests sab paths cover karte hain: `test_order_processing_happy_path` (4 effects), `test_retries_with_backoff_then_success_effect_once` (flaky card, attempt 3, charge effect 1), `test_non_retryable_failure_runs_compensation` (declined -> `{"reserve": 1, "release": 1}`), `test_saga_compensation_when_shipping_fails` (`{"reserve", "charge", "refund", "release"}` sab 1).
